speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement on postal symbols following some questions asked in the house.
I must say that my first statement took about 14 pages, but as on motions we are not entitled to speak at length I will summarize it in about four pages.

Mr. Speaker, on October 14 I was asked a question by the hon. member for Wellington South regarding the intention of the Post Office Department with respect to a symbol, to which I made the following reply: "We are going to adopt an emblem which will represent a totally Canadian post office and which will give a real interpretation to the Post
Office Act." This answer was based upon a question evidently founded on an article in the press based on information which had come from the Post Office Department to the effect that consideration was being given to the adoption of a distinctive symbol for the post office.
I regret the misunderstanding which has arisen because of this premature article of action being considered in the department, but on which the government had up to that time no opportunity to take any decision.
Shortly after I became Postmaster General I asked myself whether a symbol could not be developed which would be easily recognized as the symbol of the post office, and which would be simple to recognize and easy to reproduce. The officers of the department were receptive to the idea, and a good deal of thought and effort has been given in the department to developing such a symbol. In fact there are a number of symbols that have been used in the Post Office Department for a number of years, one of which is the hat badge of the letter carriers, which is made up of the intertwined letters "C" and "P", surrounded by a circle of maple leaves and topped by a crown.
The first step in the development of a new symbol was the use of a print of the hat badge to decorate the cover of a recruiting brochure directed at university students. This led to the use of the intertwined letters "C" and "P" and the 11 point maple leaf from Canada's flag. The stylized maple leaf, by the way, has formed part of the uniform shoulder flashes since 1965. This symbol combined with the words "Postes Canada Post" seemed to me very suitable.
I made inquiries to find out whether there was any statutory provision or any provision by order in council regarding post office emblems, and I found that neither the governor in council nor parliament appeared at any time to have prescribed such emblems, and that the emblems and other descriptions in use had been adopted by the department as a matter of usage.
Notwithstanding the practice in the past, it is my view that the latest proposal is a matter of such a nature as to require cabinet
9064	COMMONS
Announced Removal of Coat of Arms approval. However, before I had any opportunity to submit the matter to cabinet for approval, the article on which I believe the question was raised in the house appeared in the newspapers. I expect that such consideration will be given shortly.
I want to make it very clear that there was no intention on my part or on the part of the department to hide anything or to do anything without the proper authority. Certainly no such accusation can properly be made against the government, because my colleagues knew nothing about the matter up to the time the story appeared in the press.
I think I made it clear that the object of the proposed new symbol now under consideration is merely to provide a symbol of the post office which would be uniform for postal purposes and would be clearly and exclusively identified with the post office. There was no thought and no intention of interfering with the proper use of any existing symbol, and certainly no thought whatever of any kind of disrespect for the Canadian coat of arms.

He said: Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I would not say anything on such a motion because I would not think it necessary. However, on account of certain events which happened last Thursday I believe I should inform hon. members more fully about the facts of the motion.
The fact is that the committee on justice and legal affairs has had referred to it a number of important matters including motions by private members relating to the installation of safety devices on motor vehicles. We have also had two public bills, proposed by hon. members of this house, imposing upon the automobile industry punitive measures. We have heard from witnesses solely on one side of the subject, and the subcommittee in its wisdom decided that we should send a letter to the automobile manufacturers in Canada inviting them, if they so

[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

I shall not read it in full, Mr. Speaker, but in the first paragraph they suggest that there should be a common and joint interest in the committee and in the association in dealing with the subject. They commented on the fact that they had received the notices of motions and had read the members' proposed bills. They also said they had a two-day meeting in Ottawa, arranged by the Canadian government specifications board, on similar subjects.
The third and most important paragraph in the letter read as follows:
In these important matters of public interest we suggest it would be desirable if the committee members could plan a visit to the research and development laboratories and centres of the industry in the Detroit area. Such a personal visit would provide the committee with the best opportunity of learning first hand what safety activities are undertaken by the industry. It would provide a more meaningful concept of what is planned for the future. Further, it would give the members an opportunity to talk with experts in the many and varied safety subjects to which the committee refers.
The letter went on to point out that similar visits proved of value to legislators in other jurisdictions, and said they believed the same useful benefit would attach to our committee if it went to Detroit. They also offered to make the necessary arrangements for such a meeting if we decided to take advantage of their offer.
At a recent meeting of the committee when we had the Canadian Automobile Association officers before us, whose sole concern is automobile safety, they suggested it would be a wonderful idea for the committee if it could take advantage of this offer. Then the members of the committee decided in their wisdom that they probably should take advantage of the offer and go to Detroit if this could be arranged. This first step was unanimously supported by members representative of all parties in the house, and I had the necessary report prepared asking permission of the house for the committee to make this visit.
Apparently the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and members of the press thought that this was an all expenses paid

trip. It is nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker. The manufacturers offered to plan for our trip, and the visit by the committee would take a day and a half.

Such a situation is completely inconsistent with the principle applicable in this case: A man is paid by those for whom he works. In the present circumstances, I


would not dare apply that principle or explain that saying.
Somewhat along the same lines, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a precedent which may not have gone that far, but which nevertheless gave rise to a discussion in the committee on external affairs. There was some question at that time of certain people of Rhodesia who had invited the Canadian parliamentary committee on external affairs to go to Rhodesia at their expense. The Rhodesian government was ready to pay the delegates' expenses. The proposal was deemed unacceptable, because members of that committee wondered how they could make unbiased and honest judgments if they were to go there at the expense of their hosts.
The same thing applies in this case, since the problem is similar.

One cannot imagine this Canadian parliamentary committee going to Detroit on a trip, the expenses of which will be paid by the automobile manufacturers, to make inquiries and investigations in respect of the matters before the committee. If the parliamentary committee decides this trip is necessary as a business trip-I imagine it is and I will admit that point-then it is the duty of the Canadian government to pay the expenses of these parliamentarians so that they will not be subjugated by anybody else but will be in a position to do their job without any obligation and without having to undergo any brainwashing. They should be able to go there entirely free. If they are to go there to do a job for the Canadian public, they should be financed by the Canadian people and not by the United States Automobile Manufacturers Association. According to an article by Roger Newman which appeared in the Globe and Mail of today, October 25, each of these companies made approximately $500,000, or a total of $1 million. This is a scandalous and shocking situation. The taxpayers of Canada have been shortchanged by $1 million by means of tax evasion. This should be sufficient reason for proceeding at once with the debate. I submit it is urgent that we adjourn the proceedings of the house at this time to allow for a full debate on this complex treaty and its effects on the Canadian people.
You may say that debate is not urgent, Mr. Speaker, because this shocking evasion of the payment of duty happened approximately six months ago or in the spring of this year at a time when the Studebaker Company was still in operation. However, I would remind you, sir, that only yesterday we learned of the existence of this avenue of evasion. Indeed, we tried to find more about it by asking questions of the minister but we were ruled out of order. We should like to know how many more loopholes there may be in this treaty, and I think it is urgent that we find out.
If Your Honour should rule that this debate is not urgent because the Studebaker Company is no longer in business, may I submit for your consideration that what has taken place may affect other Canadian manufacturers who are still in business. What we should consider therefore is not the fact that the Studebaker Company is out of business but the fact that these regulations apply to the companies which are now in business and that the loopholes in them may be utilized. This is what we wish to find out by means of a full-scale debate.
Every day that goes by may cause the Canadian taxpayers to lose more money, and this is another reason for the urgency of this debate. We want to know what other deals may have been made, for the purpose of evading the tariff, under the treaty which allows cars to be imported from any country of the world as long as car manufacturers have export credits.
Mr. Speaker, while Nero fiddled Rome burned and, similarly, while parliament fiddles 3,000 men in Oshawa are out of work. It is therefore urgent that we discuss this matter so as to discover ways of helping these people. I think it is superfluous to point
Motion jor Adjournment out that this matter is of national importance because we all know that this treaty affects every Canadian citizen regardless of whether or not he drives a car. We should therefore be allowed to debate this important issue at the present time.
May I say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I hope Your Honour will rule in favour of the urgency of this debate on the basis of the points I have brought to your attention because, first, the auto treaty has been used to evade the tariffs; second, an evasion of this sort must not be allowed to continue any longer and, third, we want to know whether there are any other loopholes in this treaty which would permit such evasion. Thousands of men have lost their jobs owing to this treaty and I think it is very urgent that we do something in regard to it. I therefore hope Your Honour will rule that this matter is urgent and is of national importance.

As I see it, the house and the country have suddenly become aware of certain facts. Whether the house and the country should have been aware of those facts some months ago is beside the point. We have suddenly become aware of certain facts which have created a sense of confusion and a certain amount of consternation. The simplest of common sense calls for a statement to be made to a mature parliament to get the matter cleared up.
Unfortunately our rules do not permit this kind of problem to be dealt with adequately on the orders of the day. I do not think it could have been dealt with by a statement on motions because all that would have happened would have been a statement from the government side and four speeches from this side. We seem therefore to be faced with only one other choice, and that is a debate under standing order 26. It is unfortunate that it is usually assumed that if a question under standing order 26 is allowed, there goes the day. That is not necessarily the case. It is possible, and on occasions it has happened when a motion has been allowed under standing order 26, for the house to deal with the matter before it for two to three hours, clear it up and get on with its regular business. I think we need something between what can be accomplished on orders of the day and a full day's debate. I believe we could have that under standing order 26.
Yesterday Your Honour gave the benefit of the doubt to an hon. member who had raised a question of privilege. I think Your Honour ought to do the same today. Inquiries of the Ministry discussing a matter of urgent national importance, namely, the right of the government through the Minister of Industry to give in writing permission to the Studebaker Company of Canada to enter into a deal and to use the Canada-U.S. car treaty as a means of avoiding paying approximately $1 million duty on Volkswagen cars imported into Canada. member is to read two paragraphs of my reply to the telegram, which are as follows:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, October 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Eachen for the second reading of Bill No. C-227, to authorize the payment of contributions by Canada toward the cost of insured medical care services incurred by provinces pursuant to provincial medical care insurance plans.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: If the minister speaks now, he will close the debate. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the minister is waiting with restrained anticipation to conclude this debate. Coming into the debate at this late hour, there are one or two
October 25. 1966

matters that I am going to deal with which have not as yet-as I have read the record of the debate and followed it in the house-received full attention. I say at once that the various members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition who have spoken in the course of this debate have dealt with the matter of medicare in a manner that in my estimation has brought honour to them. The study that each of them has made of the problem and the devotion of this party to the principle of medicare have resulted in a continuing demand by members of this party for action to implement a medicare plan that is not a sham and a delusion but a practical, legislative enactment.
The view of our party in regard to the need of a national medicare plan, because the provinces have the entire legislative and constitutional responsibility for health, is that the provinces should be consulted. A plan should be arrived at not by the compulsory edict of a minister or a government but by consultation and agreement. Plans should be practical and practicable, not an instrument which has all the appearance of providing medicare but fails to take into consideration the responsible and reasonable position taken by several of the provinces.
On December 21, 1960, as reported at pages 1023 and 1024 of Hansard, I announced in the house that the government had decided to set up a royal commission, the scope of whose authority and the personnel of which would be announced early in the new year, to investigate this matter thoroughly. On June 20, 1961, as reported at page 6600 of Hansard, I announced the setting up of the royal commission with the task of looking into the field of medicare, assuring that the government would have the fullest information so that whatever plan was brought into effect would have behind it the information and research necessary. Appointed to head that royal commission was, of course, Mr. Justice Hall, and representatives from across Canada were appointed to it. There were two medical representatives on the commission, Dr. Arthur Van Wart of Fredericton and Dr. David Baltzan, chief of staff of the Department of Medicine, Saskatoon, and one of the outstanding authorities in Canada on the subject of medicare and medical assistance.
Out of that commission came a report which was widely acclaimed; indeed, it was described by various newspapers and commentators as a health charter. The Toronto Star, which has never been a transcendent admirer of the Conservative party, stated in
Medicare
an editorial on June 20, 1964, that when the royal commission on health services was set up in 1961 sceptics suspected that it was intended as a delaying device to enable the government of the day to postpone decision on a national health plan. The editorial also said that the commission's report, which had been released that week, triumphantly refuted these suspicions. It said that the report was a landmark in the history of Canadian welfare programs and if carried into effect would give Canada one of the most advanced systems of public medical care in the world.
The program has not been carried into effect. This government made promises about what it would do. Throughout the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)-and this is a matter that was stressed over and over again-said that medicare would be brought into effect by July 1, 1967. The Prime Minister's speech prepared for delivery on September 21, 1965, stated as follows:
Our objective is to have full medicare in operation on Canada's 100th birthday, July 1, 1967. We need a mandate to realize this objective.
They got the mandate and returned to office, although one of the ministers was lost in the shuffie because he made a wrong prediction as to the outcome of the election. What has happened since September, 1965, in the economic life of Canada? What changes have taken place that make impossible the carrying out of this program?
As recently as July 14 the minister answered a question asked by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) in these words:
Mr. Speaker, we propose to proceed with the medical care program in accordance with the bill which is now available to hon. members.
Then the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked the following question:
-I wish to ask the Prime Minister whether he has had any opportunity to consider the appeal I made to the government last night to give consideration to proceeding with second reading before the house adjourns for the summer recess?
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The Prime Minister replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I read my hon. friend's statement on this subject, but we propose to follow the plan that has been outlined and proceed with second reading of the legislation shortly after our return.
That legislation, and I have the bill before me, provided for the commencement of the plan on July 1, although there was a joker in

October 25, 1969
Medicare
it. One of the clauses of the bill was obviously placed therein for the purpose of providing an outlet for their refusal to carry out the undertaking. I would like very much to know the meaning of clause 6 which states:
It is a condition of payment of any amount as or on account of a contribution by Canada to a province for a year in respect of a medical care insurance plan of the province
(a) That the provincial authority will (i) on or before the first day of July, 1967 or the date of commencement of the plan, whichever is the later, in the case of the year that includes the later of those dates-
None of us took that provision seriously. We believed the Prime Minister and we believed the ministers.
But what has happened to the economic situation in Canada in this last year to cause the government to break its pledged word? The promise that was made was a most solemn one. The government expected to break this promise, they had it in mind. I am not exaggerating when I make this statement because on January 11, 1966 a well known journalist wrote the following:
The betting in Ottawa is that a national medicare plan, now scheduled for unveiling July 1, 1967, will be postponed until after centennial year.
The article from which I quoted was written by Maurice Jeffries who today is on the outskirts of a cabinet position. Farther on he said:
The recent report of the Economic Council of Canada, stressing what governments and business must do in the immediate period ahead to maintain generally prosperous conditions and provide for the rapidly growing labour force, has led to second thoughts on the timing of medicare.
This journalist knew that but parliament did not. Sir, the action of this government in deluding and deceiving the Canadian people cannot be countenanced. Again, I quote a Liberal member of the Ontario legislature from a publication the name of which is "Liberal Action." It reads as follows:
The federal cabinet's decision to delay medicare for one year is a shocking breach of faith with the Canadian people.
This was said by James Trotter, M.P.P. in an interview and it was the view of quite a number of Liberal members when they made their pilgrimage to Peterborough. You will remember, sir, that in the old days in England pilgrimages were the order of the day. Some pilgrims went to Canterbury and others went to Peterborough, but the interesting fact is that those who went to Peterborough were the growlers who were not satisfied with things in general. This Liberal aggregation, [Mr. Diefenbaker.l
which I understand, included parliamentary secretaries and even ministers went there and said: "Not over our dead bodies". They are still alive because they have been told to stay alive. The breaking of an agreement means nothing to this government. Their explanation is that if this plan were brought in now it would bring about inflation. Well, we have inflation now and the plan is not in effect. So that was an excuse.
I may say, sir, that the minister is a charming fellow but after having read his speeches on what he was going to do I am surprised to see him sitting where he is. He made grievous threats and there were sounds of rivalry in the cabinet, as reported in the press. He said he was going to resign, that this was the last straw. But he is still there.
It was interesting to listen to his opening speech because for mildness and sweet compassion no speech by any other minister has ever equalled his performance. He was mild and restrained; he had a contrite heart and he revealed it in the lachrymose way in which he delivered his speech on second reading. He said: "Let there be medicare on July 1, 1967". but he was overruled by the strong man of the cabinet today. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) said: "You are not going to get this. I am not going to allow it." I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) is a man who carries out his promises and when I say that, I may add conjunctively that we all recall the $25 million promised in Nova Scotia. When I went to Cape Breton the Nova Scotians said to me: "We were promised $25 million and we are going to have the mine opened." This was another promise that was not carried out.
What does the government say now? They say: "We broke our word. We fooled the Canadian people. What we will do is put the plan into legislation now and we will keep our word." What guarantee have we that the pledged word of the government will be carried out because it is in legislation? What was the excuse? The Minister of Finance said, and all who listened were impressed: "We have canvassed painstakingly every possible way of meeting our commitment to medicare and our responsibility for the stability of the economy and the soundness of our finances." What happened to these finances and to the stability? Have things slipped so badly?
The minister said it did not appear to him they could pay for medicare, a guaranteed
October 25, 1966

income for the aged and the established programs of the government in the same year. He said they had to observe priorities. We have been asking them about priorities. What has happened to the priority of the old age pensioners? Day after day hon. members, including the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) have repeatedly asked for an assurance. They asked the government: "What is going to be done for the old age pensioners?" The answer was: "Wait and see. If only you get through this legislation we will go ahead with it." And yet they have not got it on the order paper.
Had we been elected we would have carried out our promises as we have done in the past. The reason the Liberals have not done so is that the economy has deteriorated and they could not carry out their promises. That is the excuse. They had not established any priority. Why should this house allow itself to be fooled? The people of Canada are being deceived. This is paper medicare, a post-dated-cheque medicare. This is not legislation, it is prophecy. In a year and a half from now they prophesy, if this parliament passes the legislation, we will have medicare.

Now I return to the subject. We in this party have taken a stand on behalf of medicare, namely the acceptance of the principle. Personally I believe the stand in favour of the principle should be taken among our members, although there will be a wide diversity of opinion as to method. Those coming from Alberta will feel that the Alberta plan is fine. Since I became leader of this party we have followed the course of change based on need. Changing conditions deserve new concepts. We believe that the Hall Commission gave a message to all Canada, and we in this nation must not allow any of our people to be subjected to a denial of the best medical attention. That was admitted by the Minister of Finance when, in his exculpatory paragraph at the Liberal meeting he said that a terrible thing faces some poor people, namely the possibility of overwhelming medical expenses and the like. should the house so decide, he will not stand stubbornly against necessary amendments but that he will show that flexibility, that capacity for compromise and retreat that characterized him in recent days as he went through a period I can only describe as one of deep mental concern, weighing the alternatives between becoming a backbencher or continuing to occupy the august position of Minister of National Health and Welfare.

October 25, 1966

subtopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am fully aware that this debate has carried on for a considerable length of time. I have not participated in it except at the resolution stage, and I have only a few brief remarks to make at this time.
In the debate we have often heard this bill referred to as a medicare bill. As I understand it, in no way can this legislation be termed as such, nor is it claimed to be such by the minister. It is an act to authorize the payment of contributions by the federal government to the provinces, to ensure services, amounting to approximately half the cost of medical practitioners' fees.
We are dealing with a very limited health insurance bill which we acknowledge is a step toward the medical health insurance which we all recognize must be available to all Canadians, according to their needs.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Second, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reemphasize once more that I am not against the principle of health insurance. For many years we in this party have advocated a system of health insurance that will make available to all Canadians adequate health care according to their needs, and not according to what might be their ability to pay. We are 100 per cent in support of the proposition that health care must be available to each citizen according to his need, regardless of his financial ability to pay.
What I disagree with, and this is the point I wish to develop briefly this evening, is the contention that it is the responsibility of the state to provide health insurance for everybody whether he wants it or not, whether he needs it or not. I do not see why it is necessary for government to assume the responsibility of providing health insurance for people who do not want it, for people who are perfectly able to take care of themselves and who want to take care of themselves. To impose the suggested type of health service on the Canadian people is to interfere seriously with the right of freedom of choice. This should in no way detract from our responsibility to assure that each citizen may have the best care when it is needed; and on that score comprehensive health insurance must be available for all Canadians.
Many speakers have justified their intention to vote for or against this bill on the ground that second reading merely represents a vote on the principle contained in the bill. If the principle were the provision by the federal
Medicare
government, in co-operation with provincial governments, of comprehensive health insurance, I would agree that that is a legitimate principle, and I could not help but be in support of it. In view of what this bill contains, and I must interpret its principle on that basis, I cannot agree with those who say they must give carte blanche acceptance to what they think is the principle.
I know that there are many differences of opinion on this matter. I know that in the party led by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) there are those who feel one way and those who feel another way, and this I can understand. Because of this difference of opinion it is very difficult for anyone to stand up and say this is, or this is not the principle of the bill. Both within my own party and within the ranks of the other parties I respect these differences of opinion.
I believe that on an issue such as this hon. members must vote according to their convictions, and I only wish all members of the house would do so. Certainly I know that within the ranks of the Liberal party there are many who have reservations about this bill, but are prevented by caucus discipline from expressing their personal convictions.
When he introduced the bill the minister laid stress on four fundamental points, and I wish to refer to them briefly because it is on the basis of some of them I find myself unable to accept the principle of the bill in relation to what it actually contains. The minister very carefully attempted to argue that universal coverage should not be confused with compulsory coverage, but this is something with which I cannot agree, unless he can enlighten us with some further explanation. His explanation that universal coverage does not mean compulsory coverage was, to me, not much more than an exercise in semantics.
What could be more compulsory than a requirement that practically the entire population of a province must be covered in order for that province to qualify for the financial assistance provided by this proposed legislation? It outlines a figure of 90 per cent coverage, rising to 95 per cent, and I think the minister would be much wiser to lower that qualification in the initial years.
If he wishes to include the plans in existence in Alberta, B.C. and Ontario, with perhaps some minor adjustments to them, it would be much wiser if universal coverage were defined as 80 per cent of a province's population in the first year of operation, 85

October 25. 1966
Medicare
per cent in the second year and 90 per cent in the third year. If the government retains this 90 per cent initial provision, then I am afraid this bill will bar from its operation three health schemes which are presently working well and which are acceptable to the majority of the people in three provinces.
I understand that a fourth province, Manitoba, is planning to introduce a scheme similar to the ones in operation in Alberta, B.C. and Ontario. We can also assume that Quebec will introduce its own plan, and if this bill remains unchanged it will thus eliminate half of the provinces from the benefits it is designed to distribute. If in the preliminary years the universal definition were lowered so that existing provincial plans could fit into the scheme, than it could not be called a compulsory plan in the same manner as it is now.
The demanded high coverage ceiling will mean the inclusion of a lot of people who do not want to come under a health insurance scheme such as this, many private insurance schemes which are presently operating satisfactorily will be eliminated, as well as schemes provided by industrial organizations and other organizations covering large groups of people. Why upset the status quo, when it is working satisfactorily for large numbers of people?
The minister also outlined the position with respect to the provision relating to public carriers, and said that in order to be acceptable a provincial health insurance plan must be administered by a public body. There are many ways in which carriers can be transformed into public carriers, making them non-profit organizations and subject to public audit by provincial legislatures; but by this provision the minister is wiping out the multi-carriers and many private carriers who now function effectively. To impose this as a qualifying requirement seems unreasonable, and I cannot accept the principle involved. In the first case that I have mentioned there is involved the freedom of choice of the individual, and in the second case the right and responsibility of a province to develop its own health plan suitable to its own needs. I have sufficient confidence in our provincial administrations that I believe they are better able to determine what kind of health insurance scheme is suited to their province than is any federal government.

[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The minister made two other points, and I should like to comment on these briefly because I find myself in partial disagreement with them. The minister has said that this legislation is limited to paying half the cost of the services of physicians. I presume he means by this medical practitioners. He estimated that cost to be $28 per capita, half of which is $14. It seems to me that if this legislation really is intended to cover the cost of health care in so far as those who administer health care are concerned, then it would not be so confining as it is. Why does it not include dentists; why does it not include optometrists, chiropractors and osteopaths? These are licensed professions rendering health service. Certainly if we are to take care of the over-all health, as it relates to health services, we cannot separate the care of the eyes, the teeth, and the specialized care given by the chiropractors and osteopaths.
I think therefore this legislation is much too restrictive. It does not accomplish what it gives the impression it intends to accomplish. Certainly it should be more inclusive. This afternoon I received a telegram-and I believe most members of the house must also have received it-from G. P. Holton, president of the Ontario Division of the Canadian Chiropractic Association urging that clauses 2 (d) and (f) of Bill C-227 be amended to include chiropractors. I am sure the discrimination to which he refers would also include optometrists, dentists and osteopaths as well. I expect this will be considered very carefully at the committee stage and that there will be amendments proposed in this regard to various clauses in the bill. At the present time I cannot agree to the bill in its limited form.
There is just one other point I should like to make. This refers to the fourth point made by the minister relating to the matter of portability. I agree that portability is absolutely essential if we are to have any kind of satisfactory health insurance scheme across the nation. However, with the three major provincial schemes, which are very similar, with another soon to be introduced, and with Quebec introducing a plan on its own, there can be portability. So far as the provincial governments are concerned, I am sure they want to accomplish and will accomplish this. Therefore it should be included, because unless there is portability we will be moving toward discrimination of another type.
October 25, 1966

I should like again to place on the record the fact that I am in favour of a national health insurance scheme which will guarantee to every Canadian the best health services that can be provided, regardless of ability to pay. However, I cannot accept the principle of the bill unless in his closing statement the minister might be able to clear up some of these things. I hope that he will. I should like him to give assurance that when we reach the committee stage the restrictive aspect of the bill so far as health practitioners are concerned will be changed, if it is the decision of the committee that it should be changed.
I believe that if, at the committee stage, the minister were willing to accept changes in this regard the bill would pass without any difficulty so far as an amendment is concerned. I believe also that if the minister would include in his statement a guarantee that it is the intention of the government through this legislation to recognize the basic plans already in existence and those which may come into being, and perhaps indicate that he would accept a lower percentage coverage in his definition of universality, it would be possible to agree to the principle of this bill. As the bill stands now however it is not possible for me to support it, having regard specifically to those principles which are enunciated in the bill itself. Again I am referring to the freedom of choice, first of all of the individual as to whether or not he wants a government health insurance plan; second, concerning which health service it will be; and third, freedom of action so that the various provinces can develop their own health insurance plans, which will reach the same objective as I am sure the minister has, in that we must have a health insurance scheme that will adequately meet the needs of the Canadian people.
So, with those remarks, I would just say again it is my hope that in his closing remarks in the debate on second reading the minister will indicate some willingness to consider some of these points which have been made both in my remarks and in the remarks of others, so that this bill will better meet the responsibility we have of ensuring that there is adequate health care for Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I want to deal for a moment with the issue of compulsion in this bill. The idea has been promoted
October 25, 1966

that this is a compulsory plan, which is an undesirable feature, and that this is something new which has been imported into the legislation. The issue of compulsion can only arise, first, with respect to the financing of the program by a province; second, with respect to physicians practising within a medical care insurance plan and, third, with respect to patients. I should like to deal with each of these categories.
A province wishing to finance its share of medical care insurance through general revenue will automatically make available the services to all the citizens in that province, and there is no compulsion there whatsoever. Later I will mention the course that has been followed in the field of hospital insurance by certain provinces.
If a province decides to finance its share of the cost of medical care insurance by levying premiums on the residents of the province, then compulsion does arise in precisely the same way that it would arise in the levying of any other tax on the population of that province. To suggest that we are embarking on a new compulsory technique in any method followed by a province is really to raise a red herring that has no place in a serious debate on medical care insurance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are asking for a 90 per cent participation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
That is the issue with respect to financing. What about the physicians who may be involved in a medical care insurance plan? The arrangement between the doctors or the medical profession and the province is obviously a matter for consultation between the two parties. However, what we are proposing in this legislation will make it possible for any physician to practise outside the plan if he so wishes. He will have full freedom to practise outside the plan, as do physicians with respect to certain medical care insurance plans now in operation in Canada. The full freedom of the physicians is protected in any traditionally required way by the medical profession, and the medical profession placed a great emphasis on the permissive character of this legislation which would allow them to practise outside the plan.
We have met them on that point. Naturally I do not think that in any province this will be widely exercised by the medical profession, but it is a right which they wish to have
Medicare
and which I think they can have without affecting the operation of the plan.
With respect to patients, no patient will be obliged to use the services of any doctor if he does not want to. He will be free to choose his doctor. Certainly the proposals in this bill make it possible for any province to adopt the arrangements that I have outlined. There is nothing in the bill which denies or prescribes the principle of voluntary choice by the patient or by his doctor. This is permissive legislation. It gives the provinces wide choice in setting organizational and administrative patterns. Its purpose is to carry out the Hall Commission objective of providing adequate medical coverage to all residents of Canada. The methods by which the provinces themselves execute this objective is within their own discretion. As in the hospital insuran.ce program, universal coverage is automatically achieved in the provinces which do not use a premium system, and there is no issue of compulsion whatsoever. Financing by premiums for hospital insurance is used in only three provinces at present. Thus in seven provinces coverage is automatically universal for hospital care.
If provincial governments choose to use similar methods of financing their share of costs then, under this legislation, all the residents of these provinces will be automatically covered. In provinces using premiums, universal coverage may be achieved through imposing premiums on a compulsory basis, as is now the case with hospital insurance in Saskatchewan and Manitoba or on a partially voluntary basis such as now applies under hospital insurance in Ontario. As I understand it Ontario collects premiums, in industrial operations having 15 or more employees and the remainder is made up from general revenue. Therefore the Ontario Hospital Insurance program illustrates how a premium province can use a voluntary system of financing to achieve universal coverage.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I ask, Mr. Speaker, in view of the experience in hospital insurance, why hon. members opposite insist on attributing compulsion to these proposals? Ontario has achieved 99 per cent coverage under the Ontario Hospital Insurance Plan through a combination of voluntary and compulsory enrolment. This course can be followed by any province under these medical care proposals, if the province so decides. In any event, this program does not require any individual to take the benefits if he does not wish to do so under

either approach. The freedom of the patient to choose the doctor, and the doctor to choose his patients, remains unimpaired under all circumstances so far as our legislation is concerned. Neither does the legislation prohibit a doctor from practising outside the scheme if he so chooses. So, Mr. Speaker, I think if we consider carefully the issue of compulsion we ought to recognize that it constitutes no serious impediment to the institution of medical care plans in any province in Canada.
May I turn for a moment to the question of medical manpower and personnel? We admit, naturally, the necessity for more doctors and additional personnel in all the health professions. Ideally, we will never likely have a sufficient supply of personnel and facilities. This will be a continuing demand that we will strive to meet and that will never be fully met. The experience has been that the establishment of a new program will stimulate efforts to increase the supply and will help focus attention on how to establish priorities in the allocation of our limited resources.
The same argument was used in the case of hospital insurance. I recall at the conference of ministers of health, the late Dr. Dumont from New Brunswick, said to his colleagues at the conference that, if the argument now applied to medical insurance had been applied to hospital insurance, Canada would not have hospital insurance as it now exists. We went ahead with hospital insurance. The fact that we took that step stimulated further efforts to create facilities and the result is we have one of the finest hospital insurance systems in the whole world.
The Hall Commission gave very serious attention to the argument made by members, especially of the official opposition-an argument that was imbedded in their amendment -to the effect we should not proceed until we had adequate supplies of medical personnel and sufficient research. The Hall Commission considered that argument and suggested that any shortage of personnel existing in this field should not act as a deterrent to the institution of medical care plans. The Hall Commission study was the most serious study ever undertaken in this field in Canada. This is the conclusion to which the Commission, came:
While we are aware that shortages of physicians, dentists, nurses and other paramedical personnel will make it difficult to establish the full personal health services program our charter envisages, none

the less the fact there are shortages must not be used as an excuse to delay initiating programs and plans.
We accept that conclusion of the Hall Commission. This argument about inadequate personnel is usually made and has been made by the official opposition, too, in their proposal, "Let us not have universal medical care now, but let us have a partial program bringing in those not presently covered or those in need of medical care." On the one hand, we argue that we have not enough doctors and, on the other hand, we advocate a partial program to cover only those not presently covered or to provide medical services for those not now receiving medical services. Well, the total position is contradictory.
This aspect of the matter was dealt with by the Hall Commission. The conclusion of the Hall Commission on this point must be related to the proposals made in the amendment moved by the official oppostion and also to the recent proposal made by the Canadian Medical Association, that we ought to take a step now to include additional millions of persons not presently receiving medical services.

I merely wish to quote a paragraph from the Hall Commission report on this point, which is a conclusive answer, it seems to me, to this particular line of argument. The Hall Commission report reads as follows:
Proponents of the voluntary approach consistently made the point that their objective is 100 per cent coverage of the eligible population under a voluntary basis. Their intention and their hope-repeated many times in the public and professional press- is that everyone could be covered and this coverage would be complete at the present time, provided all potential members had the good sense to enrol with a voluntary plan.
Implicit in the proposal of the medical profession and implicit in the amendment moved by the official opposition, is the idea that, today, doctors are now capable of meeting all of the needs of all Canadians for medical services on a prepayment basis. You cannot advocate bringing in those not now covered, as the partial plan implied, to give total medical services for all the population, and argue in the same breath that we have not got enough doctors to institute a universal program of medical care. You cannot have it both ways. I am not asking the house to have it both ways. What we say is that we
October 25, 1966

believe we ought to make a start; that any shortages existing should not be a deterrent. Once we have made a start, it will stimulate further efforts to increase facilities and personnel. This has already been the experience.
Before 1 move on to that question, I want to make the further point that the Hall Commission examined the doctor population ratio in a number of countries, including the United Kingdom, France, West Germany and Sweden. These countries have a less favourable doctor population ratio than Canada, and yet they have instituted a prepaid system of universal medical care. Our situation is better than certain countries that have already taken this step. But we are not content to regard the present situation as desirable. Through the health resources fund, we have already established a program by which we can increase the expenditure of federal funds on capital facilities for the training of health personnel. We expect this will result in an increase in medical schools and other facilities for the health professions. This parliament has committed $500 million for these purposes. That $500 million, combined with the expected share from other sources of $500 million, means a total commitment by this country of $1 billion designed to increase capital facilities for the training of health personnel.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
At the present federal-provincial conference we are considering further measures to assist higher education in Canada. This will have its effect in meeting the opportunities for medical schools and medical education. We are increasing our expenditures on research, and that will have its effect as well. So I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are moving ahead in a proper way with respect to our medical care insurance program.
Now I want to deal for a moment with the question of partial plans and with why the proposals which have been made in the house in support of partial plans are not the answer. As I recollect it, the official opposition moved an amendment asking the government to make immediate provision for those persons who are unable, for financial reasons, to provide medical services for themselves. That was their policy in the amendment that was moved. That is a partial medical care plan. It is a medical care plan for the needy. It is a medical care plan with a means test.

The definition includes drugs, dressings, prosthetic appliances and any other items of health services necessary to, or commonly associated with, the provision of the specified service. I had not intended making political or parliamentary comments in this part, but I excuse myself because the provocative speech by the Leader of the Opposition was bound to stir up a reply in the vein in which he discussed this subject matter. I appreciate the poignancy with which the Leader of the Opposition attempted to delineate the anguish and mental torture surrounding cabinet decisions and disagreements. I appreciate his poignancy, because he ought to be a past master in resolving internal disagreements and cabinet problems.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: But not pulling the rug from under your feet.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: I want to say three things about the official opposition: first, that their conduct in this debate has been irresponsible and inconsistent.
Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: Second, that the attitude they have taken in this debate has represented a sharp break with the policy laid down by their leader; finally, that they have presented a very confused picture to the house in the course of this debate-a very confused picture indeed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: "Mirror, mirror on the wall".

speechtext: We are not Liberals; that's for sure.

The Progressive Conservative party will institute a system of medicare, based on a universal, comprehensive program of medical and health services for every Canadian, as outlined in the Hall Commission report.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, October 18, I asked a question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to this effect:
Since the Canada Assistance Plan became law in July of this year, retroactive to April, can the minister advise the house why the provincial officials who administer the plan at Brantford, Ontario, have not been advised of the existence of the plan, because they are refusing to attend to cases referred to them under this plan, stating they have not received instructions about it?
Mr. Speaker, I asked this question because I believe a rather serious situation prevails in Ontario and certainly at Brantford. Less than two weeks ago I referred one or two cases, which I had thought most surely would come within the provisions and scope of the Canada Assistance Plan, to the officials at Brantford who are charged with the administration of this act. These are provincial officials. I wish to assure members of the house that these persons are competent officials. At all times in the past they have given prompt attention to cases which I have referred to them. They are dedicated. I do not wish to cast any aspersions against them in the discharge of their duties.
I should like to know from the minister, however, why it is that months after the passage of this legislation implementing this plan these provincial officials disclaim any knowledge of the existence of the Canada Assistance Plan? These matters involve cases of need. They are cases which come within the scope of this legislation. They are cases which never would have come within the scope of any welfare legislation which existed in the province of Ontario or within the scope of any federal act which was applicable in our province prior to the implementation of the Canada Assistance Plan.
This legislation now has been passed by parliament, and I am sure this house will be quite concerned about why, in my province of Ontario the government, its officials and employees still even at this late time in the year, although well aware of the nature of the Canada Assistance Plan-they were aware of it long before it ever was introduced
October 25. 196B
into this chamber-are neglecting to administer the act. Welfare officials cautioned members of parliament not to kill this bill when it was brought before us, not to destroy the bill, and now they are not implementing its provisions.
Because on behalf of my constituents, I am anxious to ensure early application of the principles of this bill, and because I am anxious to see it truly available to every Canadian family, I ask the minister tonight why the plan is not being put into effect.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Mrs. Margaret Rideout (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: CANADA ASSISTANCE PLAN-BRANTFORD, ONTARIO-REPORTED REFUSAL TO SERVICE APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question by the hon. member for Brantford I would emphasize that he was quite right in noting that the Canada Assistance Plan was enacted in July of this year with retroactive effect to April 1. I should point out, however, that the plan is a federal-provincial measure through which support is provided to strengthen and extend public assistance and welfare services programs in the provinces. Thus, while the federal government can make the funds available under the plan, the implementation of specific programs is dependant upon provincial and municipal action.
The hon. member will appreciate from the nature of the legislation that it requires the development of regulations and also of federal-provincial agreements. In order to achieve the greatest possible degree of agreement on the direction in which the plan should develop, intensive discussions have been held with all provinces since the enactment of the legislation. The regulations are now in the drafting stage and it is anticipated that they will be completed and agreements signed within the next few weeks.
In the meantime we are able under the terms of the plan to pay additional funds to the provinces in respect of mothers' allowances. The hon. member will be interested to know that the province of Ontario has received some $5 million in this way since the enactment of the legislation.
The provinces have, of course, been free to proceed at any time with the development of programs that will come within the scope of the legislation, since provision is made for retroactive reimbursement. Some provinces have, indeed, done this. Ontario, for example, took steps in this direction during the last session of its legislature when it passed the family benefits act which, I understand, will soon be in effect. This is a comprehensive 23033-5771
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion measure which will provide benefits on the basis of need for persons now covered under a number of separate programs, including old age assistance, blind persons allowances, disabled persons allowances, mothers' allowances and widows' pensions.
I hope that these comments will serve to clarify the situation with respect to the question raised by the hon. member for Brantford.

TELEVISION-SUGGESTED CURTAILMENT OF BROADCAST OF GREY CUP GAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate, and I must say that I am a little bit relieved by the fact that the Secretary of State is not in the house. The last time I engaged in a debate with her I came out so badly and there was such confusion that medicare almost got through second reading without anybody knowing about it.
The point of my question relates to the duplicate coverage, for some 80 per cent of the Canadian public, of the Grey Cup football game. When I raised this matter initially, perhaps because of the way I phrased my question, there were some who thought I was against football and others who thought I was against beer. Fortunately those who know me will never accuse me of the latter, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that at the proper time in November I will be watching the Grey Cup game and drinking beer. I hope that no one will call me to interrupt me during those sacred hours.
The fact is that it is ridiculous in this country to have one event telecast by two television stations, with one commentator during the game for both stations, and another during the colour follow-up program. Let me add that the same commercials will be telecast to this effectively built-in captive audience. I hope that when Ottawa beats the best of the west by 24 to 13, nothing like this duplication of broadcasting will be permitted.
Perhaps I am being optimistic in this hope because nothing can be done to change the situation at this time, but we as parliamentarians are going to have to have a meeting of minds, so far as our views are concerned before, during and after the game, to prevent this from occurring in the future. In the meantime I raise my small voice against this type of broadcasting. I do so because it is a broadcasting principle which effectively provides a captive audience for both the game and the commercials.

9116	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
If we are going to play up this game, largely played by American mercenaries in Canada, and consider it as a great national sport, it would be better for the C.B.C. and the C.T.V. channels to get together to broadcast and televise this game on a co-operative basis. That type of endeavour would at least make some sense.
Sir, the remedy that I suggest is a poor one, and let there be no mistake about this. I do not think you should legislate against a nuisance; you should try to make those who cause the nuisance see common sense and regulate the nuisance themselves, rather than attempting to have legislation put on the order paper and putting it in the hands of the charming minister to deal with.
We do not want any hocus-pocus in this field. A better answer is that the C.B.C. and C.T.V. get together, not as they did a couple of years back but by coming up with a common sense answer, whether it be that one network broadcasts the game one year, and the other the next year, or whether the national network broadcasts the games in their entirety.
This is the obvious answer. If this is not done, we as parliamentarians should unite behind the minister, the C.B.C. and the C.T.V.-and above all, the Board of Broadcast Governors, which is supposed to fill the heads of that corporation with the sawdust of common sense-with suggestions for not permitting such an intolerable situation to develop. Then thousands of mothers, children and non-football fans of this country will rise up and call us blessed; and as far as the football fan males are concerned, they cannot watch two football games at the same time.
I told the minister before she left this evening for the dominion-provincial conference that tonight I would be nothing but kind to her and her parliamentary secretary; but we as parliamentarians must have regard for the wishes of the people of this country. In raising this question I do not think anybody in Canada would fault us for standing up once in a while for common sense.

Mr. Speaker, on October 19 last the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) asked the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) a question in regard to duplicate coverage of the Grey Cup game by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the C.T.V. network. As we can see by the remarks of the hon. member this evening, he

DEBATES	October 25, 1966
is not satisfied with the answer given him that day. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this evening I have to give the hon. member the same answer as that given by the minister.
As the hon. member may be aware, the arrangement for coverage of our national football final is part of an agreement between the two networks in regard to television coverage of the Canadian Football League. This agreement, concluded in 1962 after a somewhat unpleasant episode over Grey Cup coverage-the hon. member must remember this, because we were in opposition at that time-also provides that the C.B.C. and C.T.V. share coverage of regular season and playoff games regardless of which network or third party purchases the right to these games.
We have spoken to the Chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors about this situation and are informed that in the board's view this co-operative approach between the two networks has been a beneficial one in ensuring orderly coverage of these games. As for the Grey Cup game, I think the board's view is that this is a once-a-year attraction of such national interest as to justify coverage by both networks.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)

PENITENTIARIES-CHANGES IN SHOULDER FLASHES OF STAFF UNIFORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, I put a question to the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Pennell) concerning the new badge on the guards' uniforms at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. It seems that the badge now reading "Department of Justice" will be changed to "Penitentiary Department of Canada".
I also asked the Solicitor General whether it was true that such a change would soon be effected and whether that would not come into conflict, I dare say, with the spirit of rehabilitation in the penitentiary field.
Mr. Speaker, my question is a short one. I should like to know this evening whether it is really intended to replace the words "Department of Justice" by "Penitentiary Department of Canada"?
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I would agree to a reference to the Solicitor General of Canada, since this service comes under his jurisdiction.
I wonder, however, if it would not be advisable to improve the situation and change
October 25, 1966	COMMONS
the shoulder badge of the uniforms to "Rehabilitation Service of Canada" or something of the sort which would correspond more closely with the spirit of rehabilitation.
But for pity's sake, Mr. Speaker, let us not choose a shoulder badge on that uniform bearing the words "Penitentiary Department of Canada" I would not venture to say that it is degrading, but for those who wear it, this is not at all the same thing. While previously we had "Department of Justice" we now have "Penitentiary Department of Canada." Following my visit to St. Vincent de Paul, I heard comments in that connection and not only is this change unwelcomed but
